Watch me with *sympathy*. I see sym-, which means 'together.' I see -pathos, which means 'feeling.' And -y shows a state or quality. Put them together: 'feeling together,' or sharing someone's feeling. Now I check the sentence on page 32 to confirm it fits."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Do you know other words with sym-/syn- or path- that carry the idea of 'together' or 'feeling'?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Symphony, because instruments play together. Empathy and apathy have the feeling part. Sympathetic is the same word family."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Try *interrupting*. Inter- means 'between,' and rupt comes from a Latin word meaning 'break.' So interrupting is 'breaking in between.' Now *conscience*: con- means 'with' and sci means 'know,' so it is an inner 'knowing' of right and wrong. And *diploma* comes from a Greek word meaning 'folded paper,' which is why it is a certificate."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which word has a part that helps you guess its meaning, and what is your guess?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Interrupting. Inter- is like in 'intersection' where roads cross between each other, and rupt is like 'erupt' or 'break,' so it means breaking into what someone is doing."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Some words do not have helpful parts, such as *reeked*, *strewn*, and *nauseous*. For those, use context. Read the sentence on page 30 or 31 with me and decide: is the feeling of the word pleasant or unpleasant? That is a clue to its connotation."},{"type":"directions","text":"Add all ten words to your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer. For *sympathy*, *interrupting*, and *conscience*, mark the word parts and write what each part means. 'The sentence says ___, so I think ___ means ___.' 'This word makes the reader feel ___.'","watchFor":"If students guess only from the word's sound or one part, then prompt: 'What does the whole sentence tell you?' Make a three-column chart with the headings: Percy's mom, Gabe, Montauk memories. As you reread, annotate and record two or three details in each column. Then, at the bottom, write what each set of details shows Percy values."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"To cite evidence, I name where it is and say what the text shows. Then I make an inference by asking, 'What does this detail suggest about what Percy cares about?' For example, when Percy keeps thinking about how his mom has to put up with Gabe, that shows he is worried about her more than about himself."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Have students use the text for exact details from pp. 29–36 on Percy's mom (her work, her sacrifices, how Percy talks about her), Gabe (his poker nights, his treatment of the mom, his smell and mess), and the Montauk memories (the beach, the cabin, Percy's feelings there). Accept any accurate details students find; the sample responses below are examples."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details about Percy's mom show how Percy feels about her?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On these pages Percy talks about his mom with a lot of caring. He gets upset when she is treated badly and he wants to protect her, so he values his mom and her happiness."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details about Gabe show what Percy does not value?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Gabe is described as rude and selfish, and his apartment is messy and smells bad. Percy does not value people who take from others or who treat his mom with disrespect."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do the Montauk memories show Percy values?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The Montauk memories are calm and happy, and they are connected to his mom. That shows Percy values family closeness, safety, and freedom."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Putting these together, what does Percy value most, and what is your evidence?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy values his mom and the love and safety of family most. The text shows this because his best memories are with her at Montauk, and his anger at Gabe is about how Gabe treats her."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"Based on the details in Chapter 3, what does Percy seem to value most?","choices":[{"text":"Loyalty to and protection of his mom, and the love and safety of family","correct":true,"rationale":"This is supported by his caring thoughts about his mom, his anger at how Gabe treats her, and his happy Montauk memories."},{"text":"Winning Gabe's approval so that the apartment feels like home","correct":false,"rationale":"Percy is disgusted by Gabe, not trying to please him. This misreads Percy's feelings."},{"text":"Being popular and fitting in at school","correct":false,"rationale":"This idea fits many school stories, but these pages focus on home, family, and memories, not popularity."},{"text":"Finding out about the monsters from Ms. Dodds","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses Chapter 2's mystery with Chapter 3, whose focus is home and relationships."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in citing details and explaining inferences with precise present-tense verbs about character.","sayAsk":"Model: 'The text shows that Percy cares about his mom.' Frames: 'On page ___, the author describes ___.' 'This detail suggests Percy values ___.' 'Percy feels ___ because ___.' Have partners tell each detail aloud before writing it. Emphasize present tense for literary analysis (shows, suggests, values).","watchFor":"If students retell the plot without inferring, then ask: 'What does that detail tell us about what Percy cares about?' If students mix past and present tense, then model: 'Percy loves his mom' (present) when analyzing. Success: the student cites a page detail and states a value using a thinking verb."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Moving from a detail to an inference","tryThis":"Use the two-step prompt 'What does the text say?' / 'What does that tell me Percy cares about?' and have students answer both aloud for one detail before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Analyzing values","tryThis":"Have students explain how Percy's value of family could be a strength and a risk for a hero, using one detail from the text."}]}]},{"id":"lia-word-choice-tone","title":"Part B: Analyze Word Choice, Mood, and Tone","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.1","L.6.4","L.6.5"],"routine":"Close Read and Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 3","pages":"pp. 29–36"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Words have denotations, their dictionary meanings, and connotations, the feelings they suggest. *Reeked* and *smelled* both mean 'gave off an odor,' but *reeked* feels disgusting. Authors choose words on purpose to create mood, the feeling in a scene, and tone, the narrator's attitude."},{"type":"directions","text":"Make a two-column chart: Home (Montauk, Mom) and Gabe's apartment. Find three words or phrases for each from pp. 29–36 (for example, reeked, strewn, nauseous, and the words Percy uses for the beach and cabin). Next to each, write the connotation and the feeling it creates."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Choose one phrase describing Gabe's apartment. What connotation does it have, and what mood does it create?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Reeked has a really gross, unpleasant connotation, like something rotten. It makes the apartment feel dirty, uncomfortable, and a place you want to escape."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Now choose a phrase about home or Montauk. How do the words differ, and what tone does Percy use?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The words about Montauk are soft and warm, so the mood feels peaceful and safe. Percy's tone about home is fond and loving, but his tone about Gabe's apartment is disgusted and bitter."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do these word choices help show what Percy values?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The warm words show that he values peace, love, and family. The harsh words show that he rejects people and places where those things are missing."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Many myth heroes protect people they love and stand up to unfair rulers. How might Percy's values fit that kind of hero?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy values family and protecting his mom, just like heroes in myths who risk everything for their families or people. His dislike of Gabe's unfairness also fits heroes who stand up against bullies."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.4"],"stem":"Which best explains how the word *reeked* affects the tone and mood when Percy describes Gabe's apartment?","choices":[{"text":"It has a disgusting connotation, creating a mood of discomfort and showing Percy's disgust.","correct":true,"rationale":"Reeked carries a strong unpleasant feeling, making the setting uncomfortable and showing the narrator's attitude."},{"text":"It simply means the apartment has a smell, so it does not affect the tone.","correct":false,"rationale":"This ignores connotation; reeked is much stronger than smelled."},{"text":"It shows that Percy loves the apartment and feels at home there.","correct":false,"rationale":"This reverses the effect. The word creates a negative feeling."},{"text":"It makes the scene feel exciting and adventurous.","correct":false,"rationale":"Reeked suggests something unpleasant, not exciting."}]},{"type":"directions","text":"Quick Write (3 minutes): Write 3–4 sentences answering the text-dependent question: What do these pages show Percy values most, and how might those values fit the kind of hero we often see in myths? Use one detail about a relationship and one word choice as evidence."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students evaluate language choices and explain how connotation affects tone, using accurate verbs.","sayAsk":"Frames: 'The word ___ has a ___ connotation, which creates a ___ mood.' 'Percy's tone is ___ when he describes ___.' 'This word choice shows that Percy values ___.' Let students rehearse with a partner and compare synonyms (smelled/reeked, tidy/strewn).","watchFor":"If students say a word is 'good' or 'bad' without a feeling word, then prompt: 'What feeling does it give you? Try disgusted, calm, or cozy.' If students confuse mood and tone, then explain that mood is the reader's feeling and tone is the narrator's attitude. Success: students link a word to a connotation and a mood."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Connotation and tone","tryThis":"Offer a feelings word bank (cozy, disgusted, peaceful, tense) and a pair like smelled/reeked. Ask: 'Which word makes you feel worse? Why?' Then complete the frame."},{"type":"sample-response","text":""},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Analyzing word choice","tryThis":"Have students rewrite one sentence about Gabe's apartment using a neutral word, then explain how the mood and tone change."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students synthesize what Percy values and how word choice shows it, and connect to the Performance Task skill.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-reflection","title":"Exit Reflection","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.4"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In the Performance Task you will infer values from character description and compare them across stories. The word ___ has a ___ connotation, which creates a ___ mood. This fits a myth hero because ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Chapter 3, Percy values his mom and family, as shown when he gets upset about how Gabe treats her. The word reeked has a disgusting connotation, which creates an uncomfortable mood.
